title: Object Detection Quiz
description: Test your understanding of object detection

questions.question: What are the two main tasks that object detection combines?
questions.explanation: Object detection combines classification (determining what objects are present) and localization (determining where they are located using bounding boxes).

questions.question: In the sliding window approach, what does the 'stride' parameter control?
options: The size of the detection window
How far the window moves between positions
questions.explanation: The stride controls how far the window moves between consecutive positions. A smaller stride means more positions are evaluated (more thorough but slower), while a larger stride skips more positions (faster but may miss objects).

questions.question: What does an IoU (Intersection over Union) value of 0.7 indicate?
options: The boxes don't overlap at all
The boxes have 70% overlap relative to their union
70% of the image is covered by boxes
questions.explanation: IoU = 0.7 means the intersection area is 70% of the union area. This indicates substantial overlap between two bounding boxes. IoU values range from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (perfect overlap).

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)?
options: To remove duplicate detections of the same object
To detect objects at multiple scales
questions.explanation: NMS removes duplicate detections by keeping only the highest confidence detection for each object and suppressing overlapping detections with high IoU. This ensures each object is detected only once.

questions.question: In NMS, what happens to detections with IoU above the threshold when compared to a selected detection?
options: They are kept and the selected detection is removed
They are merged into a single detection
questions.explanation: In NMS, after selecting the highest confidence detection, all other detections with IoU above the threshold are removed (suppressed) because they likely represent the same object. This process repeats until all detections are processed.

questions.question: What does a high precision but low recall indicate in object detection?
options: Many false positives and few false negatives
Few false positives but many false negatives (missed objects)
Both high false positives and false negatives
questions.explanation: High precision means most detections are correct (few false positives), while low recall means many objects are missed (many false negatives). This often happens when the confidence threshold is set too high.

questions.question: Which of the following is a limitation of the sliding window approach?
options: Computationally expensive due to evaluating many windows
questions.explanation: The sliding window approach is computationally expensive because it must evaluate a classifier at many positions across the image. For a 100×100 image with stride 1 and window size 10×10, this means evaluating 8,281 windows!

questions.question: What is the main advantage of single-stage detectors (like YOLO) over two-stage detectors (like R-CNN)?
questions.explanation: Single-stage detectors like YOLO predict bounding boxes and classes in one forward pass, making them much faster than two-stage detectors that first generate region proposals and then classify them. This speed advantage makes them suitable for real-time applications.

questions.question: If you want to detect objects of different sizes in an image, what should you do?
options: Use a single large window size
questions.explanation: Multi-scale detection uses multiple window sizes to detect objects of different sizes. Small windows detect small objects, while large windows detect large objects. Modern detectors often use feature pyramids to achieve this efficiently.

questions.question: In object detection evaluation, what does a True Positive represent?
options: A detection that doesn't match any ground truth object
A ground truth object that wasn't detected
A detection that correctly matches a ground truth object (IoU > threshold)
questions.explanation: A True Positive is a detection that correctly identifies an actual object, typically defined as having IoU > 0.5 with a ground truth bounding box. True Positives contribute to both precision and recall metrics.
